analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy protections to teens under 18, covering nearly every company the FTC oversees.
analysis.headline: The children's and teens' online privacy bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have updated a 1998 law that protects children's online privacy. It would have expanded that law to cover teens up to age 17 and to apply to nearly any company the Federal Trade Commission oversees — including big internet platforms and phone carriers — instead of just websites aimed at kids. Companies would have needed a parent's or teen's clear permission before collecting or using a minor's data, had to explain in plain language what they collect, honor requests to see and delete that data, stop targeted ads aimed at specific children, meet written security requirements, and face lawsuits from families as well as bigger fines from the FTC. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and children under 18. Families would gain the right to know what data companies hold about their kids, to have it deleted, and to sue when it is mishandled; children and teens would get online services that cannot aim targeted advertising at them or profit from their personal information without clear permission.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the children's online privacy law from websites aimed at kids under 13 to any FTC-regulated company, including common carriers and nonprofits, that handles data on anyone under 18.

Requires parents or teens to give clear, specific consent before a company processes a minor's data — one consent per type of data, not buried in fine print — and lets them withdraw it as easily as they gave it.
Gives parents and teens the right to see what data a company has, correct it, and have it deleted within 45 days of asking.
Bans targeted advertising to a specific child based on their data or the data of similar children, and blocks companies from withholding service when a family refuses to share data.
Requires companies to delete data they no longer need, put written security plans in place, test for breaches, and agree in writing with any third party about what that party may do with the data.

Creates a private right of action with damages and attorney's fees, bars forced arbitration and class-action waivers for these claims, and raises the maximum FTC civil penalty per violation to $63,795.

analysis.who_pays: Internet platforms, social media companies, app makers, ad-tech firms, and data brokers, which would bear the cost of new consent, deletion, security, and auditing systems and lose the ability to make money by targeting ads at children and teens.

drawbacks.text: Extending verifiable consent rules to cover every person under 18 would make many websites and apps harder for teenagers to use, and some services might block young users entirely rather than comply, cutting off access to content and tools.

Compliance costs would be substantial: companies would need new written security programs, annual security reviews, plain-language privacy policies, and written contracts with every third party that touches minors' data, costs that fall hardest on small sites and nonprofits.

The bill bars companies from refusing service to a young person who declines to share data that is not essential, which limits the personalized, ad-supported business model many free internet services rely on — the cost an industry opponent would emphasize, and a tradeoff for how free online services are financed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real: children's data is mined at scale today with almost no consent or deletion rights, and this bill would have given families genuine control. The costs are real too: stricter consent and deletion rules for teen users could make some services harder to use or push sites to block under-18s entirely rather than comply, and compliance costs fall hardest on small sites and nonprofits. On balance the bill would have shifted power over children's data from ad-tech firms back to families, and it never even received a committee vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on January 29, 2020 and referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
That is the last recorded action: the complete action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote in the House or Senate.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died in committee.
The bill had five Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support on the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting and targeting advertising to minors' data kept operating under the 1998 rules, which cover only children under 13.

against.name: Internet and advertising industry
against.role: Online platforms, ad-tech, and data brokers
against.what_they_did: Broadly opposed expansion of children's privacy rules, lobbying against bills that would restrict targeted advertising to minors and create private lawsuits; no position appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never progressed far enough for a recorded vote; its five cosponsors were all Democrats, but no vote ever tested where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill bans targeted ads to specific children based on their data and requires plain-language disclosure of tracking across sites and apps. Ad targeting to minors is a major revenue source today, so this would end it.

Platforms would need verifiable consent before processing minors' data, honor access, correction, and deletion rights, limit retention, and face lawsuits from families plus FTC penalties up to $63,795 per violation. Teens under 18 are heavy users, so compliance would force real changes to how these services work.

The bill requires companies to disclose whether they sell or share minors' data with brokers and tightly limits any disclosure of that data to third parties, cutting off a market in children's information.
